title: Structs: grouping data, and what the compiler adds
objective: By the end of this lesson you can define and use structs, and you can explain why sizeof a struct is often larger than the sum of its fields — which matters as soon as data crosses a boundary.

blocks.caption: Defining and using a struct
lines: struct point q = {.x = 3, .y = 4};   /* designated initialisers: clearer, order-free */

blocks.title: Use designated initialisers
blocks.text: Writing {.x = 3, .y = 4} survives someone reordering the fields, and it states which value is which. Positional initialisation quietly assigns the wrong values the day a field is inserted in the middle.

blocks.caption: Two common styles
lines: Point p = {.x = 1, .y = 2};      /* no need to write 'struct' every time */
/* Or keep the tag, which allows self-reference: */
struct node *next;           /* a struct cannot contain itself, but may point to itself */

blocks.text: Padding: the bytes you did not ask for

blocks.caption: Same fields, different sizes
lines: char  a;      /* 1 byte, then 3 bytes of padding */
int   b;      /* 4 bytes — must start on a 4-byte boundary */
char  c;      /* 1 byte, then 3 bytes of padding at the end */
char  c;      /* 1, then 2 bytes of padding */

blocks.text: The compiler inserts padding so each field starts at an address the hardware can access efficiently. The fields are the same; only the order changed. Ordering fields from largest to smallest usually removes most of the waste, which matters when you have millions of these in memory.

blocks.title: Never write a struct straight to a file or a socket
blocks.text: The padding is invisible in your source but present in memory, and its layout depends on the compiler and the platform. Writing the raw bytes produces a file another machine may read incorrectly — and reading a struct straight from untrusted input is worse, because the padding bytes come along with whatever they contained. Serialise field by field with explicit sizes and a defined byte order.

blocks.caption: Measuring the truth
lines: printf("offset of b: %zu\n", offsetof(struct wasteful, b));
/* offsetof shows exactly where each field sits — including the gaps. */

blocks.caption: Assignment and argument passing both copy the whole thing
lines: struct point b = a;        /* a full copy — b.x and b.y are independent */
void move(struct point p);        /* copies the struct on every call */
void move_ref(struct point *p);   /* copies only a pointer — use this for large structs */
void read_only(const struct point *p);   /* and const when you will not modify it */

blocks.caption: Returning several values, and modelling a record
lines: /* A function can only return one thing — a struct is how you return several. */

blocks.caption: A union holds one field at a time; an enum names a set of values
lines: enum state { IDLE, RUNNING, DONE };      /* 0, 1, 2 unless you assign values */
};                                       /* sizeof is the largest member, not the sum */
/* A union does not remember which member you last wrote.
Pair it with an enum tag so the code can tell: */

blocks.title: Measure padding for yourself
steps: Define struct wasteful and struct tidy exactly as above
Print sizeof for both and compare
Include <stddef.h> and print offsetof for every field of struct wasteful
Reorder the fields of one of your own structs from largest type to smallest and re-measure
Define a Point with typedef and pass it to a function by value, then by pointer
Write a function returning struct parse_result and use both fields at the call site
blocks.expected: Two structs with identical fields and different sizes, offsets that show exactly where the gaps are, and a function that returns several values at once. The size difference is the lesson: the layout in memory is not the layout in your source.

cheatsheet: struct groups related fields; access with . and through a pointer with ->
Use designated initialisers: {.x = 1, .y = 2} survives field reordering
typedef lets you drop the 'struct' keyword; keep a tag if the struct points at itself
The compiler inserts padding so fields are aligned — sizeof is usually more than the sum
Ordering fields largest to smallest removes most padding
offsetof shows exactly where each field sits, gaps included
Never write a raw struct to a file or socket — serialise field by field
Structs are copied by value on assignment and on every call; pass large ones by pointer
A union is as large as its biggest member and does not remember which member is live
Pair a union with an enum tag so the code knows which member to read

checkpoint.prompt: Why is sizeof a struct often larger than the sum of its fields?

choices.A: It includes a pointer to the type
choices.B: The compiler stores the field names
choices.C: Structs always round up to 16 bytes
choices.D: Padding is inserted so each field starts at an address the hardware can access efficiently

checkpoint.explanation: Alignment requirements create gaps between fields. Reordering from largest to smallest usually removes most of them.

checkpoint.prompt: Why should you not write a struct directly to a file or network socket?

choices.A: The layout includes padding whose size and position depend on the compiler and platform
choices.B: The file would be too large
choices.C: Structs cannot be converted to bytes

checkpoint.explanation: Another machine may read it incorrectly. Anything crossing a boundary needs an explicit format: field by field, with fixed-width types and a defined byte order.

checkpoint.prompt: struct point b = a; What is b?
checkpoint.explanation: Changing b does not affect a. Structs are copied by value, on assignment and on every function call. For large structs, pass a pointer instead.

checkpoint.prompt: What is the size of a union with an int and a double member, and what does it remember?

choices.A: The size of the first member
choices.B: The size of its largest member, and it does not track which member was last written
choices.C: The sum of both, and it remembers the last write
choices.D: Always 8 bytes, and it remembers nothing

checkpoint.explanation: That is why a union is normally paired with an enum tag in a surrounding struct — the tag is what makes reading it safe.
